This is impermanence; this is the phenomenon."
If the agent and the acted-upon were non-different, then all natures would be eternal and devoid of causal nature.
Mahāmati, that all natures are without intrinsic nature yet possess a cause is not something known by the foolish and ignorant.
This refutes the externalist views.
The Buddha taught that all phenomena perceived before one's eyes are no different from impermanence; how could there be a nature that differs from its manifest entity?
Therefore, it is said: "There is no distinction between the agent and the acted-upon."

Therefore, one knows that impermanence is identical to phenomena and phenomena are identical to impermanence; since this subject and object are not distinct, they ought to possess the nature of permanence.
Regarding the absence of a causal nature, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states, "No cause is perceived," meaning that impermanence has no cause for the destruction of all phenomena.

Below the section on "all natures," the Buddha stated that the destruction of all phenomena indeed has a cause; however, this meaning is subtle and hidden, and cannot be understood by the ignorant and foolish.
"An effect does not arise from a cause that is dissimilar.
If it were to arise, then all natures would be entirely impermanent.
This dissimilarity implies that there is no distinction between the agent and the action, yet we clearly perceive such distinctions."
If intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were impermanent, it would fall into the category of being a causal characteristic (*kāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*).
If it so fell, then all natures would not be ultimate.

If all natures fell into the category of causal characteristics, then that which is itself impermanent would have to be impermanent; yet because the impermanent is impermanent, all natures would not be impermanent, and thus they would have to be permanent.
Regarding the phrase "things do not arise from dissimilar causes," this means that if impermanence were causeless, then there would be no arising of distinct phenomena.

If such arising did occur, then all phenomena would arise simultaneously with it and would all be equally impermanent. Is it not therefore certain that the existence of distinct phenomena serves as proof that impermanence must have a cause?

If it were as they conceive, then there would be no distinction between this phenomenon and that phenomenon, nor between the agent and the acted upon; yet we clearly perceive such distinct differences. How, then, can they falsely imagine that distinct phenomena arise without a cause?
If [it were argued that] "nature" is impermanent and so forth, then by definition, what is called "nature" must ultimately be unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*);
being unconditioned, it would be eternal. Since you claim it is impermanent, it falls into the category of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and thus lacks the meaning of ultimate reality.
To take this as the cause is to fall into the nature and characteristics of a causal agent, thereby losing the meaning of its intrinsic nature.

As for the statement that "if the self is impermanent, it should be impermanent," this means that if the nature of the creator were impermanent, it would follow that all created phenomena must likewise be impermanent.
If intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is itself impermanent, then the impermanent phenomena produced by it would have to be permanent.
"All natures" refers to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
"If the impermanent enters into all natures, it should fall within the three periods of time; that past form is coexistent with destruction."
In the future there is no arising, because form does not arise;
in the present, form coexists with the characteristic of decay.

As for form, it is a specific aggregation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the four great elements and their derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is indestructible, because it is free from being either different or non-different. Therefore, according to all non-Buddhist schools (*tīrthika*), none of the four great elements are subject to destruction.

All that exists within the three realms of existence—consisting of the four great elements and their derived forms—is subject to arising and ceasing among the objects of knowledge. Apart from these four great elements and their derived forms, what nature could all non-Buddhists possibly conceive of as being impermanent?
"The four great elements are unarisen, because their intrinsic nature and characteristics are indestructible.

If the nature of impermanence were pervasive throughout all phenomena, it would belong to the transformations of the three periods of time: past form has already perished, future form has not yet arisen, and present form is simultaneously perishing.

Form is the differentiated form of the four great elements; the nature of both the primary four great elements and the derivative forms is indestructible, being neither different nor non-different [from them].
All these non-Buddhists claim that the essential nature of the four great elements is indestructible in this way.
Regarding "all within the three realms of existence," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"Within the three realms of existence, there is nothing—neither the creator nor the created—that does not possess the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing. How could there be any other nature of impermanence that could produce things without itself ceasing?"
This is the Tathāgata’s refutation of the errors of the non-Buddhists:
"That which is devoid of initial creation and impermanence is not the four great elements, yet it is distinct from the four great elements.
Because each possesses its own distinct characteristic and self-nature, no differentiation can be found [between them]."
"They are without differentiation; these do not create further, nor do they act through dual means. One should know that this is impermanence.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"That which is impermanent by being created and then abandoned does not refer to the primary elements (mahābhūta) creating further primary elements, because they are distinct from one another."
It is not produced by its own characteristics, because there is no difference;
nor is it produced by common causes, because of their separation.
One should know that this is the impermanence of non-origination.
The two types of skillful means refer to the skillful means of commonality and difference, as well as further creation.
Regarding "the impermanence of the destruction of shape and location," this means that the four great elements and the derived matter do not perish; they remain ultimately indestructible.
Mahāmati! As for "ultimate analysis," it means analyzing down to the smallest atom until one observes its destruction.
One finds that the four great elements and the forms derived from them have no distinct characteristics of shape or dimension, such as length or shortness; they are not the four great elements.
"The four great elements do not perish; it is only the manifestation of their spatial form that perishes, thereby falling into the Samkhya school.

"Spatial form" refers to shape. As for the claim that the matter derived from the four great elements does not perish, non-Buddhists reckon that these primary causes and their effects are ultimately indestructible.

"Ultimately" (*zhìjìng*) means "extreme," "final," or "exhaustive. It refers to analyzing derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) down to the finest atoms (*paramāṇu*), which still cannot be further destroyed.

However, this merely involves observing the destruction of shapes, such as length and shortness, without destroying the essential substance of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives; this is merely conventional terminology, and thus it is said that "one falls into the Sāṃkhya [view]."
"Form is impermanent" means that form itself is impermanent; it is the spatial configuration that is impermanent, not the four great elements.
If the four great elements were impermanent, they would not be what is conventionally designated by worldly discourse.

If one holds that conventional discourse lacks intrinsic nature, one falls into the worldly view (lokāyata), seeing all natures as being merely verbal designations and failing to perceive their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) arising.
"Form is impermanent" means that this very form and location (*saṃsthāna*) is impermanent.
They are not the four great elements; that is to say, they do not possess the nature of the four great primary elements.

If these great elements were also impermanent, there would be contradiction and fallacy regarding conventional designations and verbal discourse. Contradiction implies they are not conventional, while fallacy implies they deviate from the ultimate truth. Thus, failing in both directions, such views are all incorrect doctrines.
Furthermore, the statement that "conventional discourse is without intrinsic nature" serves to summarize the preceding error.

"Worldly discourse" refers to the Lokāyata views of those non-Buddhists; according to their false views, all phenomena exist merely as verbal designations and lack any characteristic of intrinsic nature.
"Transformational impermanence refers to the manifestation of a different state of form (*rūpa*), not of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

It is like gold being fashioned into an ornament: there is a manifestation of transformation, yet the nature of the gold is not destroyed; rather, it is only the configuration of the ornament that is destroyed."
"In the same way, the transformation of other natures and so forth are also like this.

Regarding "the manifestation of the difference in nature of form": form refers to the form produced by the four great elements; because the substance of form undergoes transformation, its impermanent nature manifests, taking its present state as its destruction, rather than the destruction of the four great elements themselves.
Just as when gold is fashioned into various implements, the implements undergo transformation and destruction while the nature of the gold remains unchanged,
so it is with the statement that "conditioned things are subject to destruction,

yet their intrinsic nature is not destroyed. Regarding such various false imaginings of the eternalism of externalists, if the self-characteristics were not burned when the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are consumed by fire, then the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) formed from those elements would have to be severed [from them] whenever their respective self-characteristics were destroyed.
This concludes the refutation of the seven types of impermanence held by non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
All such views are based on the four great elements (mahābhūta); since they are not correct views, they are termed "erroneous conceptualizations" (vikalpa).
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"They assert that fire cannot burn the intrinsic characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) of the great elements; it merely causes them to disperse.
If it were able to burn them, then both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*) would be utterly annihilated."

That is to say, the non-destruction of the four great elements is the view of eternalism, and the dispersal of the four great elements is the view of annihilationism; all various false imaginings do not transcend these two views.
“Mahāmati! In my teaching, arising is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Why is this?

This means that because external objects are not determinate, it is taught that there is only the subtle mind of the three realms of existence; it does not speak of the arising and ceasing of various marks, nor of the distinctions of the conjunction of the four great elements, nor of the four great elements and their derivative forms. Through the two kinds of things comprised by false imagination—the grasped and the grasper—one understands these two kinds of false imagination and thereby leaves behind the two views of external existence and non-existence.
This is the Tathāgata’s manifestation of the correct teaching, which distinguishes [his position] from external views.
He says: "I teach that all phenomena arise from that which is neither eternal nor non-eternal, yet they are both eternal and non-eternal. How could such a totality possibly be employed [by others]?
The non-Buddhists are deluded regarding this and fall into the two views of existence and non-existence, as shown above.
Now, in contrast to their errors, the truth is revealed; therefore, it is said: "neither permanent nor impermanent."
The following provides a corroborative explanation.
Because external phenomena do not exist determinately, it is said that all dharmas of the three realms are manifested solely by the mind.
What is called "subtle mind" refers to the deluded mind of the present moment.
To claim that the "subtle mind" exists is incorrect.
Since one has realized that all phenomena are mind-only, there are no phenomena external to the mind; this differs from those who assert that various characteristics undergo arising and ceasing.
What are these various characteristics?
They are the distinct characteristics of the combination of the four great elements, as well as the derived matter produced by those four great elements.

For they maintain that while the great primary elements which act as producers are indestructible, the various forms which are produced are subject to destruction; yet the Buddha taught that they are neither eternal nor impermanent, meaning that they are all neither arising nor ceasing.
Regarding the two kinds of things comprised by false conceptualization—the grasped and the grasper—the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"The two natures of the grasper and the grasped all arise from discrimination."

When one can, in accordance with reality, understand that the two natures of the grasper and the grasped arise from false conceptualization, one then knows that all phenomena are mind-only, thereby departing from the dualistic views of existence and non-existence.
"When one awakens to the manifestation of one's own mind as mere representation, discursive thought arises from mental construction and activity, not from a lack of activity.

Apart from the nature of the mind, there is no such thing as the discursive thought of 'having nature' or 'lacking nature. All phenomena—mundane, supramundane, and the most excellent supramundane—are neither eternal nor non-eternal."

Failing to realize that these are the manifestations of one's own mind, they fall into a continuous succession of dualistic and evil views; all non-Buddhists fail to realize that these are their own false imaginings.

These ordinary people lack any fundamental basis, for they claim that the mundane, the supramundane, and the supreme supramundane arise from the discourse of false imagination—a truth not realized by the ignorant and foolish.
This demonstrates the characteristics of that which can cognize and that which cannot be cognized.
"Cognition" refers to the wisdom that is capable of cognizing.
From the phrase "the manifestation of one's own mind" (*svacittadṛśya*) downward, all are the objects to be cognized.
Sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been deluded regarding the essence of Mind-only—which is neither eternal nor impermanent—and thus give rise to false imaginings.
Now they realize that these false imaginings arise from the activities produced by conceptual thought; it is not that activities do not occur, for there is nothing that is not a false imagining.
Once delusive thoughts are understood, one is free from the mind’s own views of existence and non-existence.
Having abandoned these views, the essence of all phenomena—mundane, supramundane, and the most supreme supramundane—is neither permanent nor impermanent; it returns to its original state of suchness.

Those who do not awaken fall into the two extremes of existence and non-existence; their evil views continue in succession, and thus these outsiders remain constantly in conceptual construction, unaware that all is the manifestation of their own minds.

To say that ordinary beings lack a fundamental basis means that they do not know the fundamental source from which all phenomena arise; rather, they claim that all mundane and supramundane phenomena are produced solely by verbal expressions and conceptual constructions.
However, all the verbal distinctions and conceptual domains pertaining to these three kinds of dharmas are not something that ordinary, ignorant people can know or perceive.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Far removed from what is conditioned, And distinct from the various forms and locations,"
That "nature" and "form" are impermanent is the foolish delusion of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
All natures are indestructible; they abide as the great self-nature.
The non-Buddhists, with their notion of impermanence, are submerged in various views.
Those various non-Buddhists [claim] that there is neither arising nor ceasing;
the Great Nature is itself eternal. How can they speak of the perception of impermanence?
All is but the measure of mind; the two kinds of mind revolve in flux.
The grasper and the grasped—therein is neither self nor what belongs to a self.
Brahmā is the root of the tree, and its branches extend everywhere;
thus I have taught: this is merely the measure of that mind.
The first four lines provide a general verse on being free from all views.

Regarding "the various natures have no destruction," etc., this verse summarizes the preceding refutation of all views; it means that although those [natures] are falsely conceptualized as impermanent, the self-nature of the four great elements is indestructible, and thus it is said: "The great elements abide in their own self-nature."

Furthermore, the phrase "those various non-Buddhists" serves to reiterate the point regarding the non-Buddhists; it means that according to their own calculations, there is no reality of arising or ceasing, as the nature of the four great elements is eternally constant and remains as it is. How, then, can it be definitively said that they conceive of them as impermanent?
Furthermore, he demonstrates this through its essential point, saying: "All is but the measure of mind," and so forth. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"The grasper and the grasped—all are but mind; these two appear from the mind, and there is neither self nor what belongs to a self."
The non-Buddhists calculate that Maheśvara first created sentient beings as the origin of all living things, just as branches and leaves grow from a tree, pervading everything.
The Buddha said: "What I have described as the attachments of these non-Buddhists are all merely the mental constructs of their own deluded imagination."
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I pray that you will explain for me the sequential continuity of the cessation-samādhi (nirodha-samāpatti) of all bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas."

If one is skilled in the characteristics of the sequential continuity of the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), neither I nor other Bodhisattvas will ever recklessly abandon the gateway to the bliss of the meditative attainment of cessation, nor fall into the ignorance of all Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or non-Buddhists.
Regarding "extinction-samādhi" (*nirodha-samāpatti*): *samāpatti* refers to meditative absorption, specifically the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

While this samādhi is entered by all three vehicles, their respective stages and depths differ. Having understood this well, one does not abandon the Great Attainment of Cessation, yet does not fall into the attainments of ordinary beings or those of the Lesser Vehicle.
The wording of the question is clear.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Listen attentively!"
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall speak for your sake.
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that you will explain this for us.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the sixth stage, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, enter the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the seventh stage, however, enter meditative absorption in every thought-moment; they enter the absorption that is free from all signs of intrinsic nature and self-nature (svabhāva-lakṣaṇa), which is not [the domain] of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas fall into the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) that extinguishes the signs of the grasped and the grasper within the sphere of conditioned activity.

Therefore, in the seventh stage, there is no meditative attainment of mindfulness. One attains the non-differentiated characteristic of all dharmas, rather than attaining various distinct characteristics and natures; one awakens to the meditative attainment of the characteristics of wholesome and unwholesome in all dharmas. For this reason, in the seventh stage, there is no meditative attainment of wholesome mindfulness.
"Mahāmati!
At the eighth stage, the conceptualizations of mind, mentation, and consciousness are extinguished in Bodhisattvas, as well as in Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

In the answer, there are many paths regarding whether one progresses or not through the characteristics of the middle stages; all of these are explained in reference to the ten stages (bhūmis) practiced in common by the three vehicles according to the Shared Teaching (sāmānyayāna).
There are four meanings in total.

First, when comparing the sixth and seventh stages to clarify their relative depth, the sixth stage is where the three vehicles equally enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); as this level is the shallowest, the concentration attained by Bodhisattvas at this stage is no different from that of the two vehicles.

Regarding the phrase "the Bodhisattva of the seventh stage enters samādhi in every thought-moment," this means that in each and every thought-moment there is an uninterrupted entry into and emergence from samādhi. By entering samādhi while detached from all signs of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and self-nature (*svadharma*), one does not grasp at any signs of the grasper or the grasped; therefore, one does not fall into the state of active cultivation or conceptual awakening characteristic of the two vehicles.
Those who practice with discursive thought engage in conditioned activity; they must extinguish all signs before attaining meditative concentration.
Therefore, the seventh stage is called "non-recollection samādhi," meaning it is not the samādhi of abiding in recollection.
Furthermore, it is said that "attaining the non-differentiated characteristic of all dharmas" means awakening to the fact that the nature and characteristics of all dharmas have no differentiation.
"Not partially attaining" means that those of the two vehicles do not partially attain the various characteristics and natures within their meditative concentrations.
Regarding "wholesome and unwholesome": this means that when a bodhisattva reaches the seventh stage, they do not yet abide even in the wholesome, much less in unwholesome thoughts;
this is called the meditative absorption (samādhi) of being without wholesome thoughts.

Second, distinguishing the differing characteristics based on the seventh and eighth stages: this refers to the difference in the extinction or non-extinction of the delusive appearances of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), resulting in varying levels of attainment. Upon reaching the eighth stage, the delusive thoughts of all three vehicles are entirely extinguished, which distinguishes it from the seventh stage.

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from the first stage through the seventh stage contemplate the extent of the mind, mentation, and consciousness within the triple world; yet, being free from the notions of ‘self’ and ‘what belongs to self,’ they cultivate based on their own false imaginings and fall into the various characteristics of external natures.”

"Fools are ignorant regarding the two aspects of their own minds—the grasping subject and the grasped object—and fail to realize that these are permeated by the habitual tendencies of falsehood and the faults of beginningless transmigration.

Next, it clarifies that from the first stage through the seventh stage, those of the three vehicles contemplate all phenomena of the triple world as being merely mind, intellect, and consciousness; yet, although they observe in this same way, there are differences in terms of the cessation or non-cessation of delusive thought, and in terms of gain and loss.
To be free from notions of "self" and "what belongs to self" is attainment;
to fall into various external characteristics of natures is loss.

Regarding the two kinds of one's own mind: this refers to non-Buddhists who fall into the extremes of existence and non-existence, falsely conceptualizing the grasper and the grasped, being entirely ignorant and failing to realize the beginningless habituation of faults and evils.
“Mahāmati! At the eighth stage, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas [perceive] the nirvāṇa of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
However, because Bodhisattvas are sustained by the awakening of samādhi, they do not enter parinirvāṇa due to the bliss of the gates of samādhi.”

If one does not uphold it, the stage of the Tathāgata will remain unfulfilled; because all conditioned activities for the sake of sentient beings would be abandoned, the lineage of the Buddhas would consequently be severed.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, manifest the inconceivable and immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata so that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—who are led away by the attachment to the bliss obtained through their gates of samādhi—will cease to conceive the notion of [final] nirvāṇa.
3. It clarifies that in the eighth stage, the three vehicles share the same nirvāṇa, yet there is a distinction between abiding and not abiding.

Regarding the phrase "The Bodhisattva," it means that because the Bodhisattva is empowered by the power of the Buddhas' samādhi-awakening, they do not enter parinirvāṇa within the gates of samādhi for the sake of transforming sentient beings.

If one does not receive empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), one will be unable to fulfill the requirements of spiritual practice and reach the stage of a Tathāgata; this would constitute abandoning sentient beings without bringing them to liberation and severing the lineage of the Tathāgatas. Therefore, the Buddhas proclaim inconceivable merits to encourage practitioners so that they may reach ultimate perfection.

The followers of the Two Vehicles discipline themselves and deliver themselves alone; they become attached to the bliss of samādhi and give rise to the notion that they have attained nirvāṇa, and for this reason they fail. "Mahāmati!

I have divided the stages into seven, in order to skillfully cultivate the characteristics of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*); to skillfully cultivate the grasping of self and what belongs to self, as well as the person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-nairātmya*), and the characteristics of arising and ceasing, and of specific and general marks; and to skillfully master the four unhindered knowledges, the power of certainty, and the gates of samādhi, so that one may enter the successive stages of the path and the factors of enlightenment."
"Distinction" refers to the differentiation of categories, such as the distinctions between the wholesome and the unwholesome, or the ceased and the unceased.

Its purpose is to cause Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage to skillfully cultivate the characteristics of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), so that they may thoroughly understand that the nature of consciousness is fundamentally empty, thereby eliminating false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Regarding "skillfully cultivating [the realization of] 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' etc.": this means that by understanding how the two attachments to persons and phenomena encompass the two types of selflessness (*nairātmya*), one does not fall into the arising and ceasing of specific or general characteristics. Through skillful, unimpeded eloquence and the power of decisive samādhi, concentration and wisdom become equal; thereby, one gradually enters the various stages (*bhūmi*) and attains the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

"In order that Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not fail to perceive their own and shared characteristics, and do not fall onto the deviant paths of externalists due to being unskilled in the seven stages, the sequence of the stages has been established."
Mahāmati!

In reality, there is neither arising nor ceasing, apart from what is merely the manifestation of one's own mind—namely, the succession of the stages of the earth and the various activities within the triple world, which the ignorant do not perceive.
"That which is not realized by the foolish refers to my and the Buddhas' teaching on the sequential continuity of the stages (*bhūmi*), as well as the various activities within the three realms.

Regarding the phrase "not allowing Bodhisattvas [to fall]," the Buddha was truly concerned that Bodhisattvas might fail to properly discern specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and failing to understand the sequence of the stages, might fall into the deviant paths of externalists; therefore, he taught the sequence of the stages in this manner.

He further declared: "In reality, there is no such thing as arising or ceasing; the sequential progression through the stages, the transmigration through the three realms—all these are merely manifestations of one's own mind, yet the ignorant and deluded are unable to understand this."
Because they do not understand this, I and all the Buddhas have spoken thus.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and those on the eighth stage of the Bodhisattvas are intoxicated by the bliss of the cessation-samādhi; they are unskilled in the manifestation of their own minds, obstructed by the habitual tendencies of self-characteristics and common characteristics, and fallen into the views of grasping at the non-existence of persons and phenomena. They conceive a false notion of nirvāṇa, which is not the awakening of the wisdom of true quiescence.
4. It is shown that the two vehicles reach the stage of a bodhisattva and become intoxicated by the bliss of samādhi.
"Cessation" refers to the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), and that which they are "intoxicated by" is the bliss of samādhi.
Because they are intoxicated by this, they cannot properly discern that which is manifested as mind-only.

Covered by the habitual tendencies of specific and general characteristics, they cling to the two types of selflessness and grasp at views; that is to say, they cling to views regarding phenomena. Their deluded imaginings are not eliminated, and thus they conceive the notion of nirvana, which is not the true wisdom of quiescence.

“Mahāmati! A bodhisattva perceives the bliss of the gate of the samādhi of cessation, yet through the compassion of their original vow and the fulfillment of great pity, they understand the ten inexhaustible phrases of differentiation and do not falsely imagine the notion of nirvāṇa.”

Because he has attained nirvāṇa and false conceptualization no longer arises, he is free from the conceptualization of the grasper and the grasped; having realized that all phenomena are merely the manifestations of his own mind, false conceptualization does not arise regarding them. He does not fall into the mind, intellect, or consciousness, nor into the false conceptualization of clinging to the characteristics of external natures and self-natures. Not being produced by non-Buddhist causes, it arises in accordance with wisdom, whereby he attains the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization.

Regarding "the samādhi of seeing cessation" and so forth: this refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching who perceive the principle of true emptiness and nirvana; unlike the followers of the Two Vehicles who are attached to it, they maintain the compassionate vows to deliver sentient beings, practice the ten inexhaustible phrases, and do not give rise to the notion of entering nirvana.

Since one does not abide in emptiness, one is free from the grasped and the grasper; having realized that all phenomena are mind-only, one gives rise to no further discrimination and does not fall into the attachment to the intrinsic nature and characteristics of external dharmas apart from the mind and consciousness.
Since false conceptualization no longer arises, there is no further cause for rebirth; rather, with the causes for accomplishing the Buddha-dharma, one is able to reach the stage of the Tathāgata.
It is like a person who, while dreaming, employs skillful means to cross water; before having crossed, they awaken. Having awakened, they reflect:
"Was this real or was it illusory?"
It is neither correct nor erroneous.

It is the manifestation of dreams produced by the mind, intellect, and consciousness, arising from the causes of beginningless seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing; from various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and from various forms and locations that fall into the conceptualizations of existence and non-existence.

This metaphor illustrates the Bodhisattva’s method of practicing for oneself and transforming others; it means that while things are not non-existent during a dream, they do not exist once one has awakened, and thus they are neither real nor unreal.

The primary analogy is that a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage, beginning with the initial vision of ultimate reality and culminating in the liberation of sentient beings, establishes all through the illusion-like samādhi, such that their activities are like those occurring during a dream.

Upon attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), one manifests the path of effortlessness (anābhoga-mārga), such that, like awakening, there is nothing to be attained.
To say that one awakens before having crossed over is because one's stage has not yet reached its ultimate limit; one has not yet arrived at the other shore.
To distinguish between what is correct and what is erroneous is to examine their reality or unreality.
To speak of that which is neither correct nor erroneous is to exhaustively explain its underlying principle.

As for the statement regarding other things—beginningless views, hearing, cognition, consciousness, causes, thoughts, and so forth—it is intended for those remaining deluded sentient beings who, due solely to the habitual perfuming of false imaginings through seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing since beginningless time, manifest various forms and become attached to existence and non-existence; thus, these are merely the manifestations of the dream-like activities of the mind and consciousness.

“Mahāmati! In this way, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva reaches the eighth bodhisattva stage, they perceive the arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Having progressed from the first stage up to the seventh stage, and having seen that all phenomena are like illusions through various skillful means, they transcend the mental activity of conceptual construction regarding the grasped and the grasper. Thereupon, they employ the skillful means of the Buddha-dharma to cause those who have not yet attained it to attain it.”
Mahāmati!

This is the indestructible skillful means of the bodhisattvas' nirvāṇa; it is the attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) through being free from mind, intellect, and consciousness.
Mahāmati!
"In the ultimate sense, there is no sequential continuity; it is taught that all things are non-existent and that false conceptualization is quiescent.

This accords with the preceding metaphor, meaning that this Bodhisattva perceives the arising of false conceptualization, which is like the metaphor of the great river of birth and death within a dream.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) progressing up to the seventh stage, one perceives all phenomena as being like illusions and so forth; this is precisely the meaning of "skillful means" (*upāya*).

As for "having transcended the mental constructions of the grasper and the grasped," this refers to the meaning of transcending all mental constructions through one's own practice, such as the faculties and their objects.

To employ the skillful means of the Buddha-dharma so that those who have not yet attained may attain it is precisely to deliver others by means of one's own deliverance; this is also the meaning of causing those who have not yet crossed over to cross over.

Regarding the statement that "the means for attaining nirvāṇa are not destroyed," this means that although a bodhisattva has attained nirvāṇa, they do not abandon the practice of skillful means (*upāya*) for the sake of delivering sentient beings.

Regarding "being free from mind and thought" (*citta-mano-vinirmukta*), it refers to the bodhisattva reaching the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), where they attain the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*). This is illustrated by the metaphor of waking up and finding nothing to be gained; it also serves as a summary indication of the name of this patience (*kṣānti*), hence it is said: "one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Below the section on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the conclusion is presented: within the ultimate truth, which is without sequence, one speaks of sequence; within that which is without continuity, one speaks of continuity; within the absence of all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), one speaks of conceptual construction; and within the absence of the dharma of quiescence, one speaks of the dharma of quiescence.
This is because within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), not even a single dharma can be apprehended, much less a sequential continuity.

Nevertheless, all these are taught through the provisional gates of transformation according to the mental capacity of sentient beings; they are thus explained through conceptual differentiation within that which is fundamentally non-existent.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The measure of mind is non-existent; This is the dwelling and the Buddha-ground.
The Buddhas of the three periods—past, future, and present— Have all proclaimed this."
The stage of Mind-Only is the seventh; the eighth is the Stage of No-Thingness.
These two stages are called "Abiding," while the Buddha-stage is the most supreme.
Self-realized wisdom and purity—this is my own stage.
In the sovereign and most excellent place, pure and wondrously adorned,
it shines like a blazing fire; its radiance reaches everywhere,
its fierce flames do not dazzle the eyes, and its circular transformation pervades the three realms of existence.
Manifesting transformation within the three realms of existence, some may first manifest transformation there to expound the vehicles; all of these are the stages of the Tathāgata.
The tenth stage is the first, and the first is the eighth stage.
The ninth becomes the seventh; the seventh likewise becomes the eighth.
The second becomes the third; the fourth becomes the fifth.
The third becomes the sixth; when nothing exists, what order can there be?
In the first eight lines, there is first a general statement, followed by a specific one.

As for the specific: because the seventh stage still retains the "measure of mind" (*cittamātra*), whereas the eighth stage is characterized by non-existence, these two stages are contrasted to clarify their respective boundaries; thus, the name "abiding" (*vihāra*) is applied specifically to them.
"Abiding" refers to reliance.
Although the eighth stage is devoid of anything [inherently existent], it still possesses a fixed abiding; however, only the Buddha-stage is the most supreme.
The subsequent verses, beginning with "The wisdom of self-awakening and purity," all praise the stage of the Tathāgata.

"Unimpaired by its own nature" means that although the Tathāgata’s radiance is intensely brilliant, it does not, like the light of the sun or lightning, overwhelm the eyes of people when it gathers together.

"Circulating" (*zhoulun*) means to flow everywhere; it signifies that the Tathāgata flows throughout the three realms, providing inexhaustible transformation, and his transformative influence extends across the three periods of time.
"Previously" refers to the past.
"Vehicles" refers to the Great and Small Vehicles.

To speak of the ten stages as being the first stage and so forth is to manifest their perfect interfusion by means of non-sequential arrangement; yet, in ultimate terms, what stages or positions can there be for quiescent true suchness?
Therefore, it is said: "When there is nothing that exists, what sequence could there be?
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha permanent,
or is he impermanent?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is neither eternal nor impermanent;
for both positions entail faults. If he were eternal, there would be the fault of him being a creator.”
"Permanence" is what all non-Buddhists describe as a creator;
yet there is no such creation. Therefore, the Tathāgata is both permanent and impermanent, for there would be the fault of permanence being something created.

If the Tathāgata were impermanent, there would be the fault of being something produced that is impermanent; the marks characterized by the aggregates would lack intrinsic nature, and upon the destruction of the aggregates, the Tathāgata would be annihilated, yet the Tathāgata is not annihilated.

"Previously, many have spoken of permanence and impermanence, yet none have clarified whether the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata is permanent or impermanent. Speaking according to principle, how could what was previously said lie outside of this?"
If one does not clearly distinguish this, the deluded will remain in ignorance; therefore, I shall again address those who have not yet understood.

In the response, it is first stated that what is realized is neither permanent nor impermanent. This is because the principle realized transcends the hundred negations and is perfectly free from all faults, differing from the calculations of externalists; hence, it is described as a "double negation."
If one asserts that [the Tathāgata] is either eternal or impermanent, both positions entail faults.
If the Tathāgata were eternal, he would be identical to the "Self" (ātman) postulated by the non-Buddhists as an eternal creator.
The "Lord" refers to the divine self (*īśvara*).

However, when the Tathāgata speaks of "permanence," it is that which is unconditioned; therefore, it is permanent yet not [a permanence] in the sense of being permanent through action. It is not that permanence which involves activity, for such would entail error.

If the Tathāgata were impermanent, he would be something produced, identical to the five aggregates, and characterized by the marks that characterize them; since those marks lack intrinsic nature, the destruction of the aggregates would entail his cessation. However, the permanence of the Tathāgata is such that he does not cease.
“Mahāmati! All that is produced is impermanent; like jars, garments, and so forth, all would fall into the error of being impermanent.
Furthermore, the various implements and skillful means for omniscience would be rendered meaningless, because they are produced.”
All that is created should be the Tathāgata, because there is no cause for differentiation.
Therefore, Mahāmati,
the Tathāgata is neither permanent nor impermanent.
To say that all conditioned things, such as jars and garments, ultimately revert to impermanence would imply that the merit and wisdom cultivated by the Tathāgata are likewise empty and useless.
If they were identical to these conditioned things, then everything produced through effort would have to be a Buddha.
"Requisites" refers to the requisites for the adornment of merit.

Regarding "the nature of non-differentiated causes," this means that the Buddha and all phenomena share the same activity; thus, there is no separate causal nature. Therefore, it is concluded with these words.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
the Tathāgata is not eternal in the same manner as space.
If he were eternal like space, there would be the fault of rendering the various requisites for the noble wisdom of self-realization purposeless."
Mahāmati!

For example, space is neither eternal nor non-eternal; it is free from the faults of eternity and non-eternity, oneness and difference, bothness and not-bothness, and because it cannot be described due to these faults of eternity and non-eternity, the Tathāgata is not eternal.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were an unarisen permanence, he would be like the horns of a rabbit or a horse; because he would be an unarisen permanence, there would be no purpose for skillful means.
Due to this fault of being an unarisen permanence, the Tathāgata is not permanent.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
there is yet another matter by which one knows that the Tathāgata is eternal. Why is this so?
"Because the wisdom obtained immediately after the [four] truths is eternal, the Tathāgata is eternal.
Regarding the statement that the Tathāgata is not eternal in the same manner as space, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"If he were eternal, he would be like space, existing without depending on causes for his formation."
However, when the noble wisdom of self-awakening is fully manifested through the Tathāgata’s cultivation of virtue, such faults do not exist.
It further states that, for example, like empty space, it reveals the "double negation" (neither... nor... and transcends all verbal categories; therefore, it cannot be said to be permanent.

Furthermore, if it were permanent, it would be without arising; like the horns of a rabbit or a horse, which are fundamentally unarisen, there would be no principle of benefiting beings through skillful means. Therefore, it is said: "The Tathāgata is not permanent."

Furthermore, there are other matters by which one may know that the Tathāgata is eternal. Although it was stated above that he is "neither eternal nor non-eternal," this was based on his inherent qualities (*dharmatā-guṇa*) being perfectly free [from extremes].
However, since the Tathāgata has realized these qualities in accordance with their nature (*dharmatā-anurūpa*), he may also be said to be eternal.
Regarding the "wisdom obtained without interval," this refers to the unimpeded wisdom of ultimate initial enlightenment. "Mahāmati!
Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, phenomena remain definitively established."
Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all Tathāgatas dwell in the unconditioned; they do not dwell in empty space, nor is this realized by foolish ordinary people. Mahāmati!
The wisdom attained by the Tathāgata is permeated by prajñā; it is not permeated by mind, thought, or consciousness, nor by those aggregates, elements, or sense bases.
Mahāmati!
All that exists within the three realms of being is produced by unreal, deluded conceptualization; the Tathāgata, however, is not born from such unreal and deluded conceptualization.

Mahāmati, it is because of duality that there are permanence and impermanence, not because of non-duality. Non-duality is quiescence, for all dharmas lack the characteristic of arising through duality.

Regarding the phrase "whether a Tathāgata appears in the world" and so forth: this refers to the *dharmatā* realized by the Tathāgata; whether a Buddha exists or not, the characteristics of this *dharmatā* abide eternally. This principle is all-pervasive, existing without interval between ordinary beings and sages; therefore, it is called "abiding without interval."
The statement that [the Tathāgata] does not abide in empty space reveals his eternal presence; it is only because of delusion that foolish people do not recognize this.

As for the phrase "the wisdom attained by the Tathāgata," etc., it refers to the wisdom of cultivated virtue, which is entirely derived from the nature and stimulated by the permeation of *prajñā*; it is not like the mind-consciousness of sentient beings, which is permeated by the aggregates (*skandha*), realms (*dhātu*), and persons (*pudgala*).
Furthermore, it is said that the Tathāgata does not belong to the three realms, as he is not born from false conceptualization; rather, he is born solely from true and real merit.
The "two dharmas" refer to the two dharmas of birth from the false and birth from the true.

However, although within the realm of false and illusory phenomena one speaks of permanence and impermanence, these have not yet conformed to the ultimate reality; they all ultimately belong to the category of impermanence.
The ultimate reality of the Tathāgata is such that its fundamental principle is neither permanent nor impermanent.
To speak only of "permanence" is for the words to be partial while the meaning remains complete; yet the permanence realized by the Tathāgata is itself impermanence.
Because they do not comprehend this principle and instead engage in verbal discrimination between permanence and impermanence, it is said that "it is not non-dual."

However, "non-duality" refers to the principle of singular quiescence; when one investigates all phenomena to their conclusion, they are found to all possess this principle of non-duality, which is why it is said that "there is no characteristic of dualistic arising."
"Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is neither eternal nor non-eternal.
Mahāmati! As long as verbal conceptualization arises, there will be the fault of [imputing] eternity or non-eternity."

When discriminative awakening ceases, one is then free from the non-quiescence of the foolish who hold views of permanence and impermanence; the wise are eternally free from permanence and impermanence, and are not perfumed by permanence or impermanence.

This statement means that the ultimate reality realized by the Tathāgata is fundamentally free from the conceptualizations of existence and non-existence; as soon as one engages in verbal expression and discrimination, one falls into the error of the two extremes.
The cessation of discriminative cognition means that the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.
Upon reaching this state, one is free from all faults; therefore, it is said: "Eternity and impermanence are forever non-existent."

Regarding the statement that "being perfumed by the non-eternal and the eternal" is a false view—even the dual negation [of both] is a false view; if one is free from conceptual discrimination, that which is perfumed is likewise transcended.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"When the various requisites are devoid of purpose, The faults of permanence and impermanence arise."
If there is no conceptualizing cognition, whether permanence or impermanence,
then according to the thesis one has established, there will be various manifold meanings;
yet when one contemplates the measure of one's own mind, verbal expression is unattainable.

"Regarding 'the lack of meaning in all conditioned things' and so forth: this means that all those who are deluded and whose cultivated virtues have not yet manifested fall into the errors of permanence and impermanence.
If one is free from conceptual discrimination, one transcends these two extremes and proceeds toward tranquility."

Regarding "that which they establish as their thesis," this refers to the permanence and the seven kinds of impermanence as conceived by non-Buddhists; since these are nothing other than false views, it is said that "there are thus various and manifold meanings."
If one contemplates with the wisdom of a Buddha that the manifestations of one's own mind are mere mental constructs (*cittamātra*), thereby accords with the true principle;
then all conceptual discriminations and verbal expressions become unattainable. *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra-bhāṣya*, Fascicle Four, Part One.
